unit.title: The Number System
unit.blurb: Place value in whole numbers and decimals up to thousandths, multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000, and rounding decimals.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Understand the value of each digit in whole numbers and decimals with up to three decimal places.

O2.t: Round numbers with up to two decimal places to the nearest tenth or whole number.

p: Every digit has a **value** that depends on its **place**. In 4072.358 the 4 is worth 4000, the 7 is worth 70, the 3 is worth 3 tenths (0.3), the 5 is worth 5 hundredths (0.05) and the 8 is worth 8 thousandths (0.008).
A zero holds a place: in 4072 there are no hundreds.
Multiplying by 10 moves every digit **one place to the left**; dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right. × 100 and ÷ 100 move two places; × 1000 and ÷ 1000 move three places.

lesson.t: Why each place is 10 times the next
p: Ten ones make one ten, ten tens make one hundred, and ten tenths make one whole. Every place is worth 10 times the place to its right.
So the 3 in 3.45 is worth 3 ones, the 4 is 4 tenths and the 5 is 5 hundredths.
× moves digits left; ÷ moves them right.
The decimal point stays where it is; fill gaps with 0.
0.5 and 0.05 are not the same: the 5 is in a different place.

p: To round to the **nearest whole number**, look at the tenths digit. To round to **one decimal place** (the nearest tenth), look at the hundredths digit.
**5 or more**: round up. **4 or less**: round down.

steps: the hundredths digit is 7, so round up

p: Rounding to 1 decimal place asks whether the number is nearer one tenth or the next. The hundredths digit tells us.
Find the two values it is between.
0–4 round down; 5–9 round up; keep the 0 in 13.0.
4.96 to one decimal place is 5.0, because 4.9 + 0.1 = 5.0.
